## THE CURRENT MAP
75:16/q01 What does moving the tongue mean here? [تُحَرِّكْ لِسَانَكَ · meaning] (turns on: Whether the phrase denotes the organ's motion or the recitation accomplished with it.)
  75:16/q01/p1 It is the physical motion of the speech organ in reciting revelation. — reasons: Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī define taḥrīk as moving something between directions; al-Jishumī places motion and rest among spatial states. Al-Ṭabrisī calls the tongue the instrument of speech. Ibn al-Jawzī gives lisān as the organ, lasin as skilled speech, and lasan as eloquence; he also reports the simple sense 'tongue itself'.
  75:16/q01/p2 Moving the tongue stands for reciting or rehearsing the words. — reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī explicitly glosses tongue movement as recitation to preserve the revelation; al-Ṭabrisī gives the same metonymy.
75:16/q02 Which broader facts about the articulation and form of speech are cited? [لِسَانَكَ · grammar] (turns on: Which articulatory or morphological environment governs the cited speech forms.)
  75:16/q02/p1 Identical consonants may assimilate, conceal, or remain distinct according to movement, word boundaries, and word structure. — reasons: Sībawayh favors assimilation when at least five moving segments would follow, citing poetic meter; clear Hijazi articulation remains good. More movements strengthen the preference, and a preceding long vowel counts as movement, as his rhyme example with yāʾ shows. A preceding matching moving consonant and following quiescent consonant also favor assimilation. Across words, distinct articulation remains possible; a quiescent predecessor bars silencing, though concealment with moving weight is possible. Ibn Nūḥ and ism Mūsā preserve word form, unlike intra-word رد and قل. Qurādd/lahāmm cannot be silenced; poems of an unnamed poet and Ghaylān b. Ḥurayth witness concealment. Meccans reportedly do not fully pronounce both tāʾs in 58:9; thawb Bakr favors clarity. Ṣuwaym permits concealment or silence. Final long wāw/yāʾ remain unassimilated before matching initials; speakers can conceal or articulate but cannot silence without losing length, as rhyme confirms. Imperative ikhshi/ikhshū can assimilate because their glides are not long vowels. Two hamzas are normally distinct, although Ibn Abī Isḥāq's assimilation is called poor but permissible. Iftaʿala tāʾs can be shown or concealed, unlike fixed iḥmarra; some Arabs quiesce the first or move the predecessor. Al-Ḥasan's 37:10 reading and Meccan murdifīn reported by al-Khalīl and Hārūn attest alternatives; muqtalīn is rarer and radif dialectal. Initial alif is retained in ألْحمر as hamzat qaṭʿ-like. Assimilation in iqtatalū is acceptable like jaʿal laka. اردد permits no concealment between two still letters.
  75:16/q02/p2 Hamza at pause permits several realizations determined by its preceding sound and case. — reasons: Sībawayh records hinted or applied case vowels. Tamīm and Asad often move the predecessor to clarify faint hamza; some Tamīm avoid a faʿl sequence in al-radiʾ. Other Arabs replace final hamza by wāw, yāʾ, or alif by case, as in al-kalʾ/al-wathʾ. The choice should remain consistent. Once the predecessor moves, ordinary pause rules apply; final hamza is not doubled. Hijazi lightening after fatḥa yields alif without ishām; after ḍamma/kasra yields wāw/yāʾ. After a still consonant, softened hamza is deleted and its vowel transferred.
  75:16/q02/p3 Weak letters change form according to position, vowel, suffix, and pattern. — reasons: Sībawayh cites taʿayyaṭat and rajaz ʿawṭaṭ for quadriliteral yāʾ becoming wāw. Final radicals are weakest because endings bear inflection and suffixes. Wāw-final imperfects use yafʿulu, yāʾ-final yafʿilu; faʿula occurs with wāw, not yāʾ. Final wāw after ḍamma and yāʾ after kasra resist heavy endings but accept fatḥa. After fatḥa they become alif; before consonantal suffixes they retain their original identity. Declensional final wāw after ḍamma shifts to yāʾ/kasra; consonant-preceded glides behave like sound radicals. Some plurals prefer yāʾ, while wāw after kasra always becomes yāʾ, with ʿAbd Yaghūth's verse cited. An added alif hamzates a final weak radical. Dialectal ghazi/shaqi retain yāʾ; raḍiyū/sarūw depend on vowel retention and two-sukūn avoidance. Lightened hamzated jīʾ/jūyi turns to jī. Deleted weak radicals remain deleted in singular jussives; dual long-vowel markers remain while jussive nūn drops.
  75:16/q02/p4 Weak-medial noun plurals vary by vowel, number, gender, and analogy. — reasons: Sībawayh gives afʿāl for small counts of wāw-medial faʿl to avoid heavy afʿul, and fiʿāl/fiʿlān for larger counts; qaws/aqwus and rajaz athwāb preserve rarer afʿul. Yāʾ-medial faʿl likewise takes afʿāl in small counts, often fuʿūl in larger ones. Hollow qāʿ/tāj/jār favor afʿāl and fiʿlān. Yūnus reports feminine dār/sāq/nār with afʿul, but Sībawayh doubts gender alone explains it; dār/sāq also take fuʿul, dīrān, diyār. Nīb avoids yāʾ plus ḍamma. Fīl nouns use afʿāl/fuʿūl, sometimes -ah. Arwāḥ/riyāḥ preserve wāw class patterns. Feminine weak-medial nouns can take -āt or sound-like larger plurals, while nūbah/jawbah/dawlah/qaryah take broken fuʿul. Ḍayʿah/khaymah have nonregular fuʿul by analogy. Qīmah/rībah/dīmah permit sound and broken patterns; nāqah-type favors fiʿāl with fuʿul also; ʾaynūq/qiyam and the poetic tārāt/tīr are exceptional.
  75:16/q02/p5 First-person suffix and pausal pronunciation depend on host structure and articulatory pressure. — reasons: Sībawayh distinguishes verb-object -ni from genitive -ī; frequent particles may drop nūn, especially laʿallī, whereas Zayd al-Khayl's poetic laytī is exceptional. ʿAnnī/qadnī/qaṭnī/minnī/ladunnī preserve the nūn-yāʾ marker; ilā/ladā/ʿalā cannot add nūn because their endings cannot move; qaṭ/ʿan/min are fixed like verbs. Some Arabs move a prefinal consonant to avoid adjacent still letters at pause; a Saʿdī poet's al-naqri witnesses this. Vowel harmony or pattern avoidance explains ʿudl/fisl, al-busr, and al-ʿukm; long vowels in Zayd/ʿawn differ. Qalqala qāf/jīm/ṭāʾ/dāl/bāʾ release audibly, sometimes strongly; zāy/ẓāʾ/dhāl/ḍād release softer breath, and other voiceless sounds breathe. Lām/nūn/mīm/ʿayn/ghayn/hamza lack this release. Connected speech suppresses pausal releases, illustrated by ayqiẓ ʿumayran and aḥriz mālan.
75:16/q03 Who is addressed by the prohibition? [لِسَانَكَ · referent] (turns on: Whether the scene is Gabriel delivering revelation, the resurrection record, an individual's inward knowledge, or inquiry about Judgment.)
  75:16/q03/p1 The Prophet Muhammad is addressed while receiving revelation. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī and many commentators connect the command to Gabriel's delivery. Abū Ḥayyān calls this the apparent account supported by the sound occasion report. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it is etiquette during revelation.
  75:16/q03/p2 A person confronted with a record of deeds at resurrection is addressed. — reasons: Al-Qaffāl ties this to 75:13–15 and 17:14: God gathers and reads deeds, then commands confession and explains punishment. Al-Balkhī appeals to the surrounding judgment passage. Al-Jishumī says this fits what a person sent ahead better, though he says the worldly address is more apparent. Al-Suyūṭī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reject the account because of the sound revelation report and 20:114 parallel.
  75:16/q03/p3 Humanity generally is addressed about its inward knowledge or conscience. — reasons: Elmalılı reports this possible universal reading, based on 75:14–15 and the implied inner knowledge; he prefers the specific prophetic address because Qurʾān is later named.
  75:16/q03/p4 The addressee is a person asking prematurely about Judgment Day. — reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this proposal: God will gather those destined for Judgment, reveal its description, and clarify it with the trumpet blast; he rejects it.
  75:16/q03/p5 The instruction extends to every believer studying the Qurʾān. — reasons: Asad extends it to reading, listening, and studying; Study Quran says students should reflect before drawing conclusions.
75:16/q04 What does the pronoun “it” refer to? [بِهِۦ بِهِۦٓ · referent] (turns on: The unstated antecedent, identified from the revelation occasion or the surrounding resurrection passage.)
  75:16/q04/p1 The Qurʾān or revelation, though its antecedent is implicit. — reasons: Al-Wāḥidī compares the unintroduced pronoun with 97:1; Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares 38:32. Al-Rāzī allows revelation, its descent, or Qurʾān. Elmalılı prefers this because Qurʾān is named later. Al-Ālūsī likewise cites 97:1. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says concision suits the sūra's haste motif. Asad specifies the contents of revelation; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports a narrower reading of what had already been recited.
  75:16/q04/p2 The person's record of deeds or the deeds read from it. — reasons: Al-Qaffāl links the pronoun to 75:13–15 and 17:14; al-Jishumī and al-Bayḍāwī describe an anxious reader. Al-Suyūṭī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reject the interpretation by the revelation report and parallel 20:114.
  75:16/q04/p3 What is within a person, namely conscience. — reasons: Elmalılı says this follows if the address is universal and the implicit antecedent derives from the preceding self-witness passage; he prefers the Qurʾān reading.
  75:16/q04/p4 The coming Judgment and its description. — reasons: Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this interpretation and calls it untenable.
75:16/q05 What action does the verse prohibit? [لَا تُحَرِّكْ بِهِۦ لِسَانَكَ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether tongue movement is simultaneous recitation, later review, premature delivery, or a resurrection scene.)
  75:16/q05/p1 Reciting along with Gabriel before his revelation is complete. — reasons: The Prophet should listen with heart and ear and repeat only after Gabriel finishes. Al-Ṭabarī prefers Ibn ʿAbbās via Saʿīd: review for memory would be after collection, so the prohibition concerns premature recitation. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares a listener finishing a speaker's words
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<75:16 update 1, part 1 of 0..2>>
 too soon.
  75:16/q05/p2 Compulsive or continuous review after receiving revelation, from fear of forgetting. — reasons: Al-Ṭabarī records Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and al-Ḥasan on repeated review; he argues against taking that as the immediate occasion, since memory review follows collection. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says it became burdensome.
  75:16/q05/p3 Speaking or delivering revelation before its connected parts have arrived. — reasons: Al-Shaʿbī says love and the sweetness of recitation prompted this; the instruction is to wait for the connected whole.
  75:16/q05/p4 Rushing the recitation to people, who need measured repetition for the message to settle. — reasons: Al-Jishumī reports a worldly-life coherence reading: repeated, slow instruction establishes God's proofs in hearts distracted by love of the world.
  75:16/q05/p5 Rushing through one's record of deeds in distress at resurrection. — reasons: Al-Qaffāl says God reads, gathers, and explains the deeds and asks for confession. Al-Jishumī finds the preceding self-accounting context favorable; al-Suyūṭī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī dispute the report's fit.
  75:16/q05/p6 Voicing one's inner knowledge or asking too soon about Judgment. — reasons: Elmalılı reports the conscience interpretation. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports a question about Judgment and rejects it.
75:16/q06 What does “to hasten with it” mean? [لِتَعْجَلَ بِهِۦٓ · meaning] (turns on: What activity is premature and what 'it' denotes.)
  75:16/q06/p1 To try to take in or memorize revelation before its delivery is complete. — reasons: Al-Ṭabrisī distinguishes haste, action before its due time, from speed at the first due moment. Al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī gloss the phrase as hastening to receive it; 20:114 is their parallel. Al-Ālūsī says the bāʾ transitively marks what the tongue moves with or one hastens to learn.
  75:16/q06/p2 To deliver or speak the revelation prematurely out of eagerness. — reasons: Al-Shaʿbī gives eagerness to convey and sweetness of speech as the occasion; al-Jishumī's worldly reading calls for slow repetition to people.
  75:16/q06/p3 To hurry through a record of deeds, or to hurry a question about Judgment. — reasons: Al-Qaffāl links the former to the fearful reading of the record; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports and rejects the latter.
75:16/q07 How does the purpose phrase function? [لِتَعْجَلَ بِهِۦٓ · grammar]
  75:16/q07/p1 It explains why the Prophet moved his tongue; the bāʾ marks the object of his recitation or learning. — reasons: Al-Sāmarrāʾī says the purpose clause gives the cause of the motion and matches the sūra's atmosphere of haste. Al-Ālūsī calls the bāʾ transitive on both accounts, movement with it or haste to learn it.
75:16/q08 Why did the Prophet hasten? [لِتَعْجَلَ بِهِۦٓ · reports] (turns on: The reported motive: fear of loss, love and mission, questions about meaning, or the need to teach listeners.)
  75:16/q08/p1 He feared losing or forgetting the revelation and strained to secure its words. — reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās reports moving lips to catch a passage's beginning before its end, with the revelation weighing on him; Saʿīd demonstrates the movement in reports transmitted by Bukhārī and Muslim. Al-Tirmidhī grades one account ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Al-Biqāʿī adds reverence, while Farāhī adds fear of accountability for even one lost letter.
  75:16/q08/p2 He loved revelation, its sound, knowledge, and the duty of conveying it. — reasons: Al-Shaʿbī calls it love and sweetness on the tongue; al-Jishumī reports Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise. Al-Biqāʿī compares Moses' haste to please God at 20:84 and calls Muhammad's motive praiseworthy though calm reception is a higher state. Iṣlāḥī compares his urgency to a hungry child, thirsty traveler, and separated lover receiving a letter. He needed answers to opponents, spiritual and intellectual guidance, and sound mission strategy; Farāhī says this concern coexisted with memory fear.
  75:16/q08/p3 He hurried to understand the meaning and ask questions while Gabriel was still reciting. — reasons: Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Zamakhsharī's addition of questions about meaning to hurried memorization; divine preservation lets questions wait.
  75:16/q08/p4 In a worldly coherence reading, he was urged to repeat slowly so listeners could absorb the proof. — reasons: Al-Jishumī says listeners' attachment to worldly life made repeated reminders necessary.
75:16/q09 What happened after the instruction was revealed? [* · reports]
  75:16/q09/p1 The Prophet listened quietly to Gabriel, then recited the revelation as taught after Gabriel departed. — reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd imitate the former lip movement. Bukhārī and Muslim transmit multiple routes; Bukhārī says he lowered his head when Gabriel arrived. One report adds that a sūra's end became known only when the basmala descended; another says he should follow the recitation and explain lawful and unlawful matters. Al-Biqāʿī gives no grading for his transmitted report.
  75:16/q09/p2 The revelation occasion is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās and several early interpreters. — reasons: Ibn Kathīr names al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Qatādah, Mujāhid, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk; Wāḥidī names Muqātil, Mujāhid, Qatādah, and ʿAṭāʾ. Al-Tirmidhī's Ibn ʿAbbās report is graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ by al-Qurṭubī; Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and Abū Ḥayyān cite Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī.
75:16/q10 What does the instruction teach about receiving and preserving revelation? [* · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the lesson is specific to the Prophet's reception or also extends to later Qurʾān students.)
  75:16/q10/p1 Listen until the reading is complete; God undertakes collection, preservation, recitation, and explanation. — reasons: Al-Khaṭṭābī says the unlettered Prophet should attend to understanding; al-Kashshāf adds heart and ear, then repetition and study. Ibn Kathīr identifies three stages: reception, recitation, explanation. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says inna causally grounds the prohibition in the promise, comparing 9:103. Iṣlāḥī adds arrangement and divinely appointed timing; 20:114–115 exhorts patience.
  75:16/q10/p2 Patient study should precede conclusions; students must attend to meaning rather than mere fluent sound. — reasons: Asad applies the instruction to every believer, linking 20:114 to hasty conclusions from isolated verses and urging study of the whole message. Study Quran likewise urges reflection on all teachings.
75:16/q11 Does the prohibition imply a prophetic sin? [* · theology] (turns on: Whether the act was permitted before the command, a sin, or a good act refined by instruction.)
  75:16/q11/p1 The earlier haste could have been permitted until this prohibition. — reasons: Al-Rāzī answers the sin argument by analogy with a ruling changed over time, as in abrogation.
  75:16/q11/p2 The haste was either unauthorized sin or inexplicable if already permitted. — reasons: Al-Rāzī attributes this dilemma to those who permit prophetic sin.
  75:16/q11/p3 The haste sprang from a praiseworthy motive, and the command moved him to a more complete calm. — reasons: Al-Biqāʿī sees love of God and message as its motive and compares Moses' haste to please God at 20:84. Iṣlāḥī says noble motives still required patience under gradual revelation.
75:16/q12 What does this episode show about prophecy and divine agency? [* · theology]
  75:16/q12/p1 God fixed revelation in the Prophet without ordinary study, demonstrating divine preservation and authorship. — reasons: Al-Jishumī calls this a miracle contrary to ordinary experience. Al-Biqāʿī says the command unveils divine giving rather than Muhammad's composition and cites 76:30 for action under God's will.
  75:16/q12/p2 The Prophet had exceptional perception, yet receiving Gabriel's words still strained him. — reasons: Al-Biqāʿī says he was complete and continually advancing, not distracted from knowledge; he cites the Prophet's report of seeing companions behind his back, and describes sight in darkness and complete unveiling. Despite that, reverence and fear of loss prompted haste.
  75:16/q12/p3 The divine timing of revelation supplied the Prophet's mission, spiritual renewal, and answers to opponents. — reasons: Iṣlāḥī says he depended on guidance at every step, while opponents challenged piecemeal revelation and demanded replies. Revelation strengthened resolve, soul, and intellect; the Prophet was to leave collection, arrangement, explanation, and timing to God.
75:16/q13 How is this instruction connected to other Qurʾānic passages? [* · links]
  75:16/q13/p1 It parallels 20:114, which forbids hastening the Qurʾān before revelation is complete. — reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī also cites 87:6. Al-Rāzī says 20:114 redirects reliance from repetition to God and asks Him for knowledge. Ibn Kathīr notes the instruction to ask for more knowledge. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the parallel supports reports of one-time as well as staged descent. Iṣlāḥī adds 20:115 for patience.
  75:16/q13/p2 Its divine guarantee is comparable to promises of preserving, reciting, or clarifying revelation. — reasons: Al-Wāḥidī reports Abū ʿAlī's comparison to 20:114; 87:6 is also invoked for assured memory. Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares the causal use of inna with 9:103.
75:16/q14 How does the instruction fit the sūra's surrounding argument? [* · links] (turns on: Whether the command is an occasion-driven aside, a thematic transition, or part of the judgment scene.)
  75:16/q14/p1 It is a timely aside during revelation, after which the resurrection discourse resumes. — reasons: Al-Khaṭṭābī and al-Rāzī compare a teacher or speaker briefly correcting a distracted listener. Al-Suyūṭī says the opening reached 75:15 as the Prophet hastened, and 75:16–19 intervened. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it etiquette interrupting the resurrection account. Al-Rāzī says six contextual explanations answer an allegation of textual loss.
  75:16/q14/p2 It is linked thematically by haste, conscience, speech, and the need for divine guidance. — reasons: Al-Rāzī ties unbelievers' pursuit of immediate ha
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

<<75:16 update 1, part 2 of 0..2>>
ppiness to religious haste, fear of forgetting, knowledge of their own falsity, and reliance on God; Abū Ḥayyān contrasts denial of signs with the Prophet's eager preservation. Al-Bayḍāwī says even haste in religion is reproved. Elmalılı integrates conscience and revelation; al-Suyūṭī moves from the human soul to the Prophet's soul. Al-Sāmarrāʾī links the reproaching soul, spoken excuses, 75:20, omitted elements, and gathering bones and Qurʾān; he also notes plural and singular divine forms. Al-Biqāʿī ties self-reproach to the accusation of human speech at 74:25–26. Iṣlāḥī relates the instruction to pressure from opponents.
  75:16/q14/p3 The verses continue the resurrection record scene rather than introducing a prophetic aside. — reasons: Al-Balkhī and al-Qaffāl invoke the surrounding self-witness and record passage; al-Jishumī finds this contextual fit stronger while conceding the prophetic reading is more apparent. Al-Suyūṭī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reject it on the revelation report and 20:114.
  75:16/q14/p4 The seeming break prompted an allegation of missing or altered text. — reasons: Al-Khaṭṭābī records the objection that 75:16–19 separates 75:14–15 from 75:20–21. Al-Rāzī attributes alteration allegations to early Rāfiḍīs; al-Suyūṭī records a Shiʿite allegation of dropped material. Abū Ḥayyān repeats al-Rāzī's report. Al-Khaṭṭābī, al-Rāzī, and Abū Ḥayyān answer with contextual connections.
75:16/q15 How are the following verbs about loving immediate life and leaving the Hereafter read? [* · readings]
  75:16/q15/p1 The following verbs yuḥibbūna and yadharūna are read in the third person or second person. — reasons: Al-Jishumī reports the third-person reading from Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Yaʿqūb, and the second-person reading from the others.

## THE NEW NOTES
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p143/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الطيبي | reports | Al-Ṭībī says that while receiving earlier verses the Prophet habitually hurried ahead of Gabriel; at 75:15 Gabriel inspired the instruction to receive revelation properly, after which the recitation resumed at 75:20, like a teacher pausing a rushed pupil. | mentions 75:15, 75:16, 75:17, 75:18, 75:19
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p143/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Ālūsī rejects the interruption account as far-fetched and unsupported; the sound majority transmission instead treats the address as directed to the Prophet. | mentions 75:16, 75:17, 75:18, 75:19
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p143/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو حيان | reports | Abū Ḥayyān links the passage to the contrast between a denier absorbed in sinful desires and someone who preserves, studies, and presents God’s signs in hope of acceptance; opposites reveal each other.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p143/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Ālūsī objects that Abū Ḥayyān’s contrast works only after the discussion of the denier is complete, whereas the tongue instruction appears in the middle. | mentions 75:16
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p143/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · القفال | reports | Al-Qaffāl reads the command as addressing the human being when shown his record: fear makes him stumble and rush through it, so he is told not to move his tongue hastily. | mentions 75:13, 75:14
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p143/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · القفال | reports | On al-Qaffāl’s view, God promises to assemble the person’s deeds, read them to him, have him acknowledge or consider the record, and then explain its consequences and punishment; this is a severe threat of a detailed account. | mentions 75:13, 75:14
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p143/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · البلخي | prefers | Al-Balkhī and his followers prefer al-Qaffāl’s reading: the pronouns refer to the record implied by 75:13 and the sentence is circumstantial, introduced by an implied saying, at the presentation of the book. | mentions 75:13, 75:14
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p143/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · القفال | reports | Al-Qaffāl's reading that the person receiving his record is addressed differs from the authentic majority transmission that the address is to the Prophet.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p144/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | In the alternative reading, this is a prohibition on asking about the Day’s timing, framed as not opening one’s mouth to rush for its knowledge.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p144/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الإمام | reports | The Imam suggests the Prophet’s haste may have been explicitly permitted until the prohibition came; al-Ālūsī finds this account problematic.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p144/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الضحاك | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk reports that the Prophet feared forgetting the Qurʾān and reviewed it until the effort became burdensome; the report is not established and the verse’s apparent sense does not support it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p144/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | An alternative reads the direct address as the Prophet, a generic addressee, or any suitable listener; the pronoun refers to the Day of Resurrection, and the sentence interrupts the threat to intensify its terror.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p144/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | On that alternative, the passage means not to hasten to learn the Day’s timing: God will gather creation, reveal its conditions in the Qurʾān, and manifest it at the blast; demanding its date is contrary to wisdom.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p144/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Ālūsī says this alternative has serious difficulties and is not the best explanation; he points instead to Zamakhsharī’s account as fitting the Qurʾān’s eloquence and subtle indications.

<<end of input>>

item.text: The new notes mainly bear on the prophetic and record of deeds readings already in the map. Two details need their own entries: moving the tongue as an idiom for asking about the Day, and the proposed syntax of the command in the record reading.
